title: Lobes of the lungs (anterior)
attribution: 3D anatomy from Z-Anatomy, built on BodyParts3D (CC BY-SA). Rendered in Blender; surface detail added with an image model.

rows: Above the horizontal fissure and in front of the upper part of the oblique fissure.
Three segments: apical, posterior and anterior.
hy: Reactivated tuberculosis favors the apices of the lungs.

rows: Wedge at the front of the right lung, between the horizontal and oblique fissures.
Below and behind the oblique fissure.
Five segments: superior, medial basal, anterior basal, lateral basal and posterior basal.
hy: Material inhaled while upright usually reaches the basal segments of this lobe; while lying on the back it reaches its superior segment or the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.

rows: Above and in front of the oblique fissure. Its lower tongue-shaped part, the lingula, matches the middle lobe of the right lung.
Four segments: apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingular and inferior lingular.
Below and behind the oblique fissure.
Four segments: superior, anteromedial basal, lateral basal and posterior basal.
Runs from the cricoid cartilage at C6 to its division into the two main bronchi at the level of the sternal angle. The esophagus lies behind it.
Carries air to and from the lungs. C-shaped rings of cartilage hold it open, and the gap at the back is closed by the trachealis muscle.
hy: In the most common form of tracheoesophageal fistula the upper esophagus ends blindly and the lower esophagus opens into the trachea; the newborn drools, chokes and turns blue with the first feed.

rows: Runs from the division of the trachea, at the level of the sternal angle, to the hilum of the right lung.
It is wider, shorter and more vertical than the left main bronchus.
hy: Inhaled objects and fluids enter the right lung more often than the left because of the shape and direction of this bronchus.

rows: Runs from the division of the trachea to the hilum of the left lung, passing under the aortic arch and in front of the esophagus.
It is narrower, longer and more horizontal than the right main bronchus.
Runs forward from the oblique fissure at the side of the chest, along the level of the 4th rib, to the sternum.
Superior lobe from middle lobe of the right lung.
Runs from the back at about the level of the T3 spinous process, around the chest and down along the 6th rib, to the front.
Inferior lobe from the superior and middle lobes of the right lung.
Runs from the back at about the level of the T3 spinous process, around the chest and down along the 6th rib, to the front.
Superior lobe from inferior lobe of the left lung.
